slides.title: Lines in Designing a City
slides.html:
Lines in Designing a City

I can use points, lines, and planes to describe a map.

geo.title: Lines in Designing a City
geo.target: I can use points, lines, and planes to describe a map.

slides.title: Get started
slides.html:
Each pair sketches a street grid for a new town and marks where streets cross. Which streets never meet? Which corners are on one straight street?

  • I can use points, lines, and planes to describe a map.
  • I can use point, line and plane to describe a map, and say which terms are undefined.
  • I can tell when two distinct lines in a plane meet once or never.

figure.alt: Side view of a three-legged stool and a four-legged chair on a floor drawn with a front and a back edge. All three stool feet touch the floor, marked with dots. The chair stands where the floor dips slightly: three of its feet touch the floor and its front right foot hangs above the dip, with a small arrow across the gap.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.html: Point, line and plane are undefined: we describe them with rules instead of definitions. Our first rule, a postulate we accept without proof, is that through two different points there is exactly one line. A segment has two endpoints, a ray has one, and a line has none.

geo.title: The big idea
geo.body: Point, line and plane are undefined: we describe them with rules instead of definitions. Our first rule, a postulate we accept without proof, is that through two different points there is exactly one line. A segment has two endpoints, a ray has one, and a line has none.

slides.title: Words to know
slides.html:
• point An exact location with no size. We describe it but do not define it.
  • line A straight path of points that goes on forever both ways. Undefined, like point.
  • plane A flat surface that goes on forever in every direction. Undefined, like point and line.
  • collinear Points that all lie on one line.
  • coplanar Points or lines that all lie in one plane.
  • segment Part of a line between two endpoints, including the endpoints.
  • ray Part of a line that starts at one point and goes on forever one way.
  • parallel lines Lines in the same plane that never meet.

geo.title: Words to know
geo.body:
• point An exact location with no size. We describe it but do not define it.
  • line A straight path of points that goes on forever both ways. Undefined, like point.
  • plane A flat surface that goes on forever in every direction. Undefined, like point and line.
  • collinear Points that all lie on one line.
  • coplanar Points or lines that all lie in one plane.
  • segment Part of a line between two endpoints, including the endpoints.
  • ray Part of a line that starts at one point and goes on forever one way.
  • parallel lines Lines in the same plane that never meet.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Line, ray or segment?

Read the worked steps
StepReason
Start with two different points, A and B.The rule needs two different points.
Exactly one line goes through both.Two points, one line.
Segment AB is A, B and every point between them.It stops at both ends.
Ray AB starts at A, goes through B and keeps going.It has one endpoint, A.
Line AB goes on forever both ways. It has no endpoints and infinitely many points.Arrows on both ends.
Second check: C is on the same line, past B. It is already on line AB, so it does not make a new line.Still one line through these points.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Count the lines on a map.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
Four points make 6 pairs: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD.List every pair once.
A, B and C are on one line, so AB, AC and BC are the same line.Three pairs, one line.
AD, BD and CD are three more lines, all different.If two of them matched, that line would hold D and two of A, B, C. Then D would be on the street, and it isn't.
Total: 1 + 3 = 4 lines.The street line plus three lines through D.

geo.title: Worked example
geo.prompt: Count the lines on a map.

steps.step: Four points make 6 pairs: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD.
A, B and C are on one line, so AB, AC and BC are the same line.
AD, BD and CD are three more lines, all different.
steps.reason: If two of them matched, that line would hold D and two of A, B, C. Then D would be on the street, and it isn't.
The street line plus three lines through D.

slides.title: Common mistake
slides.html:
Jo says 'a line has two points: its ends.'

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Find and fix the error

Jo confused endpoints with points. A line has no endpoints and infinitely many points. A segment has two different endpoints and infinitely many points between them. Two different points determine a line; they are not the line's only points.

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
Three different markers A, B and C sit on one straight road, in that order. Think about ray BA and ray BC. Which road points are on at least one of the rays? Which are on both? What is the route from A to C that has two ends?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Rays BA and BC are opposite rays: they share the endpoint B and point in opposite directions along one line. Together they cover the whole line AC, and only B is on both. The route from A to C with two ends is segment AC, not a ray and not the whole line.

Reveal second check

A point on A's side of B is only on ray BA. A point on C's side is only on ray BC. B is on both. Those three cases cover the whole road. Segment AC also leaves out the points past A and past C.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
Mia says ray AB and ray BA are the same, because line AB and line BA are the same line. Is she right?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No. They sit on the same line, but ray AB starts at A and goes past B. Ray BA starts at B and goes past A. They are different rays.

Reveal second check

X is past B. X is on ray AB but not on ray BA. One point in one and not the other proves they are different.

slides.title: Practice 3
slides.html:
A segment has two named endpoints. Does it have only two points? Name a third point without using a distance formula.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No. Every point between the endpoints is on the segment. If the endpoints are at 0 and 6, the point at 2 is a third point.

Reveal second check

0 < 2 < 6, so 2 is between the ends, and it is not either end.
